gloss: A room or building where works of art are shown, often for sale.
examples: The *gallery* on Fifth Street shows local painters.
We spent the whole afternoon walking through three *galleries*.
Her work hangs in a small *gallery* downtown.

gloss: A public show of paintings, photographs, or other objects.
examples: The museum is putting on a big Picasso *exhibition* this fall.
Tickets for the *exhibition* sold out in a week.
Both *exhibitions* close at the end of the month.
contrast: The h is silent here: ek-suh-BISH-uhn. In the related noun *exhibit* the x sounds like gz and the h is heard: ig-ZIB-it.

gloss: An object on display in a museum, or a whole display of such objects.
examples: There's a new dinosaur *exhibit* at the science museum.
Each *exhibit* has a small card explaining it.
The *exhibits* are arranged by century.
contrast: Americans often call a whole show an *exhibit*, where the British would say *exhibition*.

gloss: An artist's finest work, or any work of outstanding quality.
examples: Everyone agrees the painting is his *masterpiece*.
The museum owns two *masterpieces* by Rembrandt.
The album was a *masterpiece* that nobody bought at the time.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A figure or object shaped out of stone, wood, or metal, or the art of making such things.
examples: A bronze *sculpture* stands in the middle of the plaza.
She studied *sculpture* for four years.
The garden is full of strange *sculptures*.

gloss: An artist who makes figures out of stone, wood, clay, or metal.
examples: The *sculptor* worked in marble for thirty years.
A local *sculptor* made the memorial by the courthouse.
Several *sculptors* submitted designs for the park.

gloss: A large sculpture of a person or animal, usually standing outdoors or in a hall.
examples: There's a *statue* of a soldier in the park.
The *statue* lost an arm in the storm.
Tourists line up to photograph the *statues*.
contrast: Three lookalikes: *statue* (STACH-oo, статуя), *status* (STAY-tuhs, статус), and *statute* (STACH-oot, закон).

gloss: A sculpture of a person's head, shoulders, and chest.
examples: A marble *bust* of the composer sits by the door.
The library has *busts* of famous writers along the wall.
He sculpted a *bust* of his grandmother from memory.

gloss: A small ornamental figure made of china, glass, or plastic.
examples: She collects little porcelain *figurines*.
A glass *figurine* fell off the shelf and broke.
The gift shop sells *figurines* of the museum's statues.
contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable: fig-yuh-REEN.

gloss: A painting, drawing, or photograph of a particular person.
examples: The *portrait* over the fireplace is of her grandfather.
He painted *portraits* to pay the rent.
It's the best-known *portrait* in the collection.
contrast: The second syllable is reduced: POR-truht, not POR-trayt.

gloss: A portrait an artist makes of himself or herself.
examples: Van Gogh painted dozens of *self-portraits*.
Her *self-portrait* won first prize at the show.
The *self-portrait* shows him at about twenty.

gloss: A painting or photograph of objects such as fruit, flowers, or bottles.
examples: She painted a *still life* of lemons and a wine bottle.
The class started with a simple *still life*.
His early *still lifes* sold for almost nothing.
contrast: The plural is *still lifes*, with -fes — never *still lives*.

gloss: A large picture painted directly on a wall.
examples: A *mural* covers the whole side of the building.
Students painted a *mural* in the cafeteria.
The city pays artists to make *murals* downtown.

gloss: A picture made by gluing paper, photographs, and other pieces onto a surface.
examples: She made a *collage* out of old magazine pages.
The *collage* hangs above his desk.
The kids glued together *collages* all afternoon.
contrast: Ends in the zh sound of *measure*, and the stress is on the second syllable: kuh-LAHZH.

gloss: A quick rough drawing made before or instead of a finished picture.
examples: He made a quick *sketch* of the bridge.
The *sketches* in her notebook are better than the paintings.
Do a rough *sketch* first, then add the color.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A picture made with a pencil or pen, or the activity of making such pictures.
examples: Her *drawing* of the horse is on the fridge.
He teaches *drawing* at the community college.
The museum owns hundreds of *drawings* by the artist.

gloss: A picture printed from a metal plate that has been cut with lines.
examples: An old *engraving* of the harbor hangs in the hallway.
The book is illustrated with *engravings*.
He bought an *engraving* at the flea market for five dollars.

gloss: A copy of a picture made by a printing process rather than by hand.
examples: She sells *prints* of her paintings online.
The original is in Paris, but I have a *print*.
Each *print* is numbered and signed in pencil.

gloss: A picture in a book or magazine that goes with the text.
examples: The *illustrations* are the best part of the book.
He does *illustrations* for children's books.
A full-page *illustration* opens each chapter.

gloss: An artist who draws or paints pictures for books and magazines.
examples: The *illustrator* worked entirely in watercolor.
She's a well-known children's book *illustrator*.
The author and the *illustrator* toured together.

gloss: A funny drawing in a newspaper, or a short animated film.
examples: The *cartoon* in the paper made me laugh out loud.
He draws political *cartoons* for a living.
The kids watch *cartoons* on Saturday morning.

gloss: A drawing of someone with certain features exaggerated for comic effect.
examples: A street artist drew a *caricature* of us with huge heads.
The magazine ran a *caricature* of the mayor.
His early *caricatures* got him fired from the paper.

gloss: A small drawing made absent-mindedly while thinking about something else.
examples: The margins of his notes are covered in *doodles*.
She drew a little *doodle* of a cat on the receipt.
My *doodles* never turn into anything.

gloss: Words or pictures painted or sprayed on walls in public places.
examples: *Graffiti* covered the wall under the overpass.
The city painted over the *graffiti* again.
Some of that *graffiti* is genuinely beautiful.
contrast: Uncountable in English: *graffiti is* everywhere — never *graffitis*.

gloss: The art of beautiful handwriting done with a pen or brush.
examples: She takes a *calligraphy* class on Tuesdays.
The invitations were addressed in *calligraphy*.
His *calligraphy* is better than most computer fonts.

gloss: A picture made of many small pieces of colored stone, tile, or glass.
examples: The floor of the church is a Roman *mosaic*.
She made a *mosaic* out of broken tiles.
The *mosaics* took two years to restore.

gloss: A heavy cloth with a picture woven into it, hung on a wall.
examples: A huge *tapestry* hangs in the great hall.
The *tapestries* were woven in Belgium.
Moths got into the *tapestry* years ago.

gloss: Colored glass held together with strips of lead to form a picture in a window.
examples: The windows of the old church are all *stained glass*.
He restores *stained glass* for a living.
Light came through the *stained glass* in bands of red and blue.

gloss: Pots, bowls, and dishes made of baked clay, or the craft of making them.
examples: She makes *pottery* in a studio behind the house.
The museum has a whole room of ancient *pottery*.
He signed up for a *pottery* class at the rec center.
contrast: Uncountable: *some pottery*, *a piece of pottery* — never *a pottery*.

gloss: An oven used to bake clay pots and bricks until they harden.
examples: The bowls go in the *kiln* overnight.
The studio has two electric *kilns*.
Something cracked in the *kiln* again.

gloss: A figure or pattern cut into wood or stone.
examples: The door has a *carving* of a lion on it.
The *carvings* on the pillars are five hundred years old.
He sells wooden *carvings* at the farmers market.

gloss: A wooden stand that holds a canvas while an artist paints.
examples: She set up her *easel* by the river.
The painting was still on the *easel*.
Two *easels* stood in the corner of the studio.

gloss: A board on which a painter mixes colors, or the range of colors used.
examples: There was more paint on his *palette* than on the canvas.
She works with a very limited *palette*.
He cleaned his *palettes* at the end of the day.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *pallet* (поддон) and *palate* (нёбо).

gloss: A brush used to put paint on a surface.
examples: Wash the *paintbrush* out before the paint dries.
She keeps her *paintbrushes* in an old coffee can.
He used the finest *paintbrush* he had for the eyes.

gloss: A single mark left on a surface by one movement of a brush.
examples: You can see every *brushstroke* up close.
His *brushstrokes* are short and thick.
A single *brushstroke* gave away the forgery.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A colored powder that is mixed with oil or water to make paint.
examples: The blue *pigment* was made from a crushed stone.
Some *pigments* fade badly in sunlight.
She grinds her own *pigment* the old way.

gloss: A painting made with paints that are mixed with water, or the paints themselves.
examples: She painted the harbor in *watercolor*.
A small *watercolor* hangs by the stairs.
He bought a set of *watercolors* for the trip.
contrast: Americans write *watercolor*; the British write *watercolour*.

gloss: A soft chalky crayon used for drawing, or a picture made with them.
examples: The portrait was done in *pastel*.
A box of *pastels* sat open on the table.
She prefers *pastels* to oil paint.
contrast: In American English the stress is on the second syllable: pas-TEL.

gloss: The person who chooses and looks after the works in a museum or show.
examples: The *curator* gave us a tour before the opening.
She's the *curator* of the photography collection.
Two *curators* chose the works for the show.

gloss: A copy of a work of art or document made to be sold as the original.
examples: The painting turned out to be a *forgery*.
He was arrested for art *forgery*.
Experts spotted the *forgery* in about a minute.

gloss: An exact copy of an object, made openly rather than to deceive.
examples: The one on display is a *replica*; the original is in Rome.
He builds *replicas* of old sailing ships.
It's a full-size *replica* of the statue.

gloss: The work of repairing an old painting or building so it looks as it did.
examples: The *restoration* of the fresco took six years.
The painting is off the wall for *restoration*.
Careful *restoration* brought the colors back.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The way the parts of a picture or piece of music are arranged, or a work itself.
examples: The *composition* of the photograph is what makes it work.
He studied *composition* before he studied color.
She has written *compositions* for full orchestra.

gloss: The technique of drawing so that distant things look smaller and farther away.
examples: The drawing is badly out of *perspective*.
Renaissance painters worked out the rules of *perspective*.
He teaches *perspective* to first-year students.

gloss: The quality of having two halves that match each other exactly.
examples: The building's *symmetry* is what makes it feel calm.
There's a rough *symmetry* to the whole painting.
She broke the *symmetry* on purpose.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable (SIM-uh-tree), but the adjective *symmetrical* on the second (sih-MET-rih-kuhl).

gloss: The part of a picture that seems closest to the viewer.
examples: A wooden fence runs across the *foreground* of the painting.
Put the tree in the *foreground* and the barn behind it.
Two small figures stand in the *foreground*.

gloss: The part of a picture that seems farthest from the viewer.
examples: The *background* of the portrait is just flat gold.
She paints the *background* first and the figures last.
The mountains in the *background* are barely visible.

gloss: The dark outline of something seen against a lighter background.
examples: The trees were black *silhouettes* against the sunset.
She cut his *silhouette* out of black paper.
You can recognize the building by its *silhouette* alone.
contrast: The h is silent and the ending is French: sil-oo-ET.

gloss: The line that shows the shape of something along its edge.
examples: Draw the *outline* first, then fill it in.
The *outline* of the mountain shows through the fog.
He darkened the *outlines* with ink.

gloss: A shade of a color.
examples: The walls are painted a warm *hue* of yellow.
The photograph has a strange greenish *hue*.
The same red turns up in a dozen different *hues*.

gloss: The difference between the light and dark parts of a picture.
examples: The photo has way too much *contrast*.
The painting gets its power from the *contrast* between light and shadow.
Turn the *contrast* down a little.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable (KAHN-trast); the verb *to contrast* on the second (kuhn-TRAST).

gloss: A type of art, music, or writing with its own recognizable style.
examples: Jazz is the one *genre* he can't stand.
The store organizes its records by *genre*.
She writes in two completely different *genres*.
contrast: Begins with the zh sound in the middle of *measure*: ZHAHN-ruh.

gloss: A skilled worker who makes things by hand.
examples: The bowls are made by local *artisans*.
He's an *artisan*, not a factory.
The market is full of *artisans* selling their own work.

gloss: The skill shown in the way something has been made by hand.
examples: The *craftsmanship* on that cabinet is beautiful.
You don't see that kind of *craftsmanship* anymore.
The price reflects the *craftsmanship*, not the materials.
contrast: Uncountable: *the craftsmanship is* excellent — never *craftsmanships*.

gloss: Decorative patterns sewn onto cloth with colored thread.
examples: The pillow has gold *embroidery* around the edge.
She does *embroidery* while she watches TV.
The *embroidery* on that jacket took months.

gloss: A frame or machine for weaving thread into cloth.
examples: She weaves rugs on a wooden *loom*.
The *loom* takes up half the room.
The old mill had two hundred *looms* running at once.

gloss: The art or practice of taking pictures with a camera.
examples: He got into *photography* in high school.
The show is all landscape *photography*.
*Photography* is not allowed in this gallery.
contrast: The stress moves: *photography* is fuh-TAH-gruh-fee, but *photograph* is FOH-tuh-graf.

gloss: A picture made with a camera.
examples: There's an old *photograph* of the farm on the wall.
She took a *photograph* of the whole crew.
The *photographs* are all from the 1940s.

gloss: A style of painting that catches the effect of light rather than exact detail.
examples: *Impressionism* changed the way painters used color.
That whole room is devoted to French *impressionism*.
He wrote a short book about *impressionism*.

gloss: Someone whose job is to judge art, music, or films in public.
examples: The *critic* hated the show, but it sold out anyway.
She works as a music *critic* for the paper.
The *critics* were kinder to his second album.

gloss: An artist who paints pictures, or a worker who paints walls.
examples: The *painter* mixed her colors on a sheet of glass.
He's a *painter* — mostly landscapes.
We hired a *painter* to do the living room.
contrast: *Painter* covers both the artist and the house painter; only context tells you which.

gloss: An object used to make music, such as a guitar or a flute.
examples: The violin was the first *instrument* she learned.
He plays three *instruments* well and two badly.
Bring your *instrument* to rehearsal on Thursday.

gloss: A stringed instrument with a long neck, played with the fingers or a pick.
examples: He's been playing *guitar* since he was twelve.
Her *guitar* needs new strings.
Two *guitars* and a drum kit filled the garage.
contrast: The stress is on the second syllable: gih-TAR.

gloss: A small wooden stringed instrument played with a bow under the chin.
examples: She plays *violin* in the school orchestra.
The *violin* was made in 1890.
Six *violins* sat in the front row.
contrast: The stress is on the last syllable and the first vowel is long: vy-uh-LIN.

gloss: A stringed instrument slightly larger than a violin, with a lower sound.
examples: The *viola* is bigger than a violin and sounds warmer.
He switched from violin to *viola* in college.
There were only two *violas* in the whole section.
contrast: Said vee-OH-luh — it does not begin like *violin*.

gloss: A tall triangular instrument with strings that are plucked with both hands.
examples: She plays the *harp* at weddings.
The *harp* has forty-seven strings.
Two *harps* were set up at the front of the stage.

gloss: A metal wind instrument held sideways and blown across a hole.
examples: She played the *flute* all through high school.
The *flute* comes apart into three pieces.
The *flutes* carry the melody in this section.

gloss: A black wind instrument with a single reed and a bell-shaped end.
examples: He plays *clarinet* in a klezmer band.
The *clarinet* squeaked on the high note.
Three *clarinets* sit right behind the flutes.
contrast: The stress is on the last syllable: kler-uh-NET.

gloss: A narrow wooden wind instrument with a double reed and a thin, sharp tone.
examples: The *oboe* gives the tuning note to the whole orchestra.
She has played the *oboe* since she was ten.
The two *oboes* open the second movement.

gloss: A curved brass wind instrument with a reed, common in jazz.
examples: He picked up the *saxophone* in middle school.
A *saxophone* solo runs through the whole song.
The band has three *saxophones* in the back row.

gloss: A brass instrument with three valves and a bright, loud tone.
examples: The *trumpet* came in loud on the last chorus.
She plays *trumpet* in the marching band.
The *trumpets* stood up for the solo.

gloss: A large brass instrument played by sliding a long tube in and out.
examples: The *trombone* slides from one note to the next.
He carries his *trombone* on the bus every day.
Two *trombones* and a tuba make up the low brass.

gloss: The largest brass instrument, which plays the lowest notes in a band.
examples: The *tuba* is the biggest instrument in the band.
He hauls the *tuba* to every parade.
The *tubas* keep the bass line going.
contrast: In American English it's TOO-buh, not TYOO-buh.

gloss: An instrument with skin stretched over a round frame, hit with sticks or hands.
examples: He plays *drums* in a cover band.
The *drum* was so loud we couldn't hear the singer.
A bass *drum* thumped all the way down the street.

gloss: A round metal plate that makes a crashing sound when struck.
examples: She hit the *cymbal* at the end of the song.
The *cymbals* crashed on the downbeat.
One *cymbal* had a crack straight through it.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *symbol* (символ).

gloss: A small drum with metal disks around the rim that you shake or tap.
examples: She shook a *tambourine* through the whole chorus.
The *tambourine* keeps the beat in that song.
There were two *tambourines* in the box of instruments.

gloss: An instrument made of wooden bars that are hit with small hammers.
examples: The kids banged away on a toy *xylophone*.
A *xylophone* plays the melody in that old cartoon.
The school owns two *xylophones*.
contrast: The x is pronounced z: ZY-luh-fohn.

gloss: A boxy instrument played by pressing keys while squeezing a folding bellows.
examples: An old man played the *accordion* on the corner.
The *accordion* weighs more than you'd think.
Two *accordions* led the polka band.

gloss: A small rectangular instrument played by blowing and drawing air through holes.
examples: He always has a *harmonica* in his coat pocket.
The *harmonica* comes in on the second verse.
She collects old *harmonicas*.

gloss: A small four-stringed instrument that looks like a tiny guitar.
examples: She learned three chords on the *ukulele* in one night.
The *ukulele* is easier on your fingers than a guitar.
They sell cheap *ukuleles* at the music store.
contrast: Pronounced yoo-kuh-LAY-lee in American English.

gloss: A wind instrument with pipes fed by air squeezed from a bag under the arm.
examples: A piper played the *bagpipes* at the funeral.
You can hear the *bagpipes* from three blocks away.
He learned the *bagpipes* from his grandfather.
contrast: Normally plural — *the bagpipes*, even when it is one instrument.

gloss: An electronic keyboard instrument that produces and shapes sounds.
examples: The whole song is built on one *synthesizer*.
He bought a used *synthesizer* off a friend.
Old *synthesizers* are worth a fortune now.

gloss: A part pressed with the foot to change the sound of an instrument.
examples: Use the *pedal* to hold the notes a little longer.
The right *pedal* on the piano sticks.
He steps on the *pedals* to change the guitar's tone.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *peddle* (торговать вразнос).

gloss: A tight wire or cord on an instrument that makes a note when it vibrates.
examples: One *string* broke in the middle of the song.
He changes his *strings* about once a month.
The *strings* come in quietly under the piano.

gloss: A device that picks up sound so it can be made louder or recorded.
examples: Tap the *microphone* and see if it's on.
She stepped up to the *microphone* and waited.
Two *microphones* were set up over the drums.

gloss: An electronic box that makes the sound of an instrument or a recording louder.
examples: The guitar plugs straight into the *amplifier*.
His *amplifier* hums whenever the lights are on.
They loaded the *amplifiers* into the van after the show.

gloss: The part of a sound system that the sound comes out of.
examples: One *speaker* is blown, so everything sounds flat.
Turn the *speakers* toward the room.
The music came out of a tiny *speaker* in the ceiling.

gloss: A device that ticks at a steady speed to help a musician keep time.
examples: Practice with a *metronome* until the tempo is steady.
The *metronome* ticked away on top of the piano.
Most phones have a *metronome* built in now.

gloss: The thin stick a conductor uses to lead an orchestra.
examples: The conductor raised her *baton* and the room went quiet.
He tapped his *baton* on the music stand.
Two *batons* lay on the podium.
contrast: In American English the stress is on the second syllable: buh-TAHN.

gloss: Very small headphones that sit inside the opening of the ears.
examples: He had his *earbuds* in for the whole flight.
One of my *earbuds* stopped working.
She pulled out her *earbuds* to hear the question.
contrast: Normally plural, like *headphones*, since they come as a pair.

gloss: The main line of notes in a piece of music, the part you hum.
examples: The *melody* stays in your head all day.
She hummed the *melody* while she cooked.
The two *melodies* are played at the same time.

gloss: Notes sung or played together with the melody to make a fuller sound.
examples: The sisters sang in perfect *harmony*.
The song is simple, but the *harmony* is not.
She sings *harmony* and he sings the melody.

gloss: The regular pattern of long and short sounds in music.
examples: The song has a strange *rhythm*.
The drums lay down a steady *rhythm*.
Caribbean *rhythms* run all through her records.
contrast: There is no vowel letter between th and m: RITH-uhm.

gloss: One of the regular pulses you count or clap along to in music.
examples: The *beat* is too fast to dance to.
Clap on the second and fourth *beats*.
He makes *beats* on a laptop in his bedroom.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *beet* (свёкла).

gloss: A series of notes that make a piece of music you can recognize.
examples: I know the *tune* but not the words.
She was whistling an old *tune*.
The band played a few *tunes* and went home.
contrast: Americans say TOON; the British say TYOON.

gloss: A single musical sound, or the written sign that stands for it.
examples: He held the last *note* for ten seconds.
She can't read a single *note* of music.
The high *notes* are hard for him.

gloss: Three or more notes played at the same time.
examples: Learn four *chords* and you can play half of country music.
The first *chord* was badly out of tune.
He struck a minor *chord* and let it ring.
contrast: The h is silent, so *chord* sounds exactly like *cord* (шнур).

gloss: The distance between one note and the next note of the same name above it.
examples: Her voice covers three *octaves*.
Try singing it an *octave* lower.
The two flutes are an *octave* apart.

gloss: A sign at the start of written music showing how high the notes are.
examples: The bass *clef* is for the lower notes.
She learned to read the treble *clef* first.
Cello music uses two different *clefs*.

gloss: A short group of beats between two vertical lines in written music.
examples: The solo starts in the fourth *measure*.
Count four *measures* of rest, then come in.
Play the last two *measures* again.
contrast: Americans call it a *measure*; the British call the same thing a *bar*.

gloss: A sign in written music that raises a note by a half step.
examples: There are two *sharps* in the key signature.
That note is a C *sharp*, not a C.
He can never remember where the *sharps* go.

gloss: A sign in written music that lowers a note by a half step.
examples: The piece has three *flats*.
Play B *flat* there, not B.
The *flats* are marked at the start of the line.
contrast: In music a *flat* lowers a note; in British English *flat* also means an apartment.

gloss: How high or low a musical sound is.
examples: She has perfect *pitch*.
His voice dropped in *pitch* at the end of the line.
The whole choir was singing under *pitch*.

gloss: The part of a song that repeats after each verse, or a group of singers.
examples: Everybody sings along on the *chorus*.
The *chorus* comes back three times.
The *choruses* are the only part I remember.

gloss: One of the sections of a song that has the same tune but different words.
examples: The second *verse* tells the rest of the story.
He wrote four *verses* and then cut two.
She forgot the words to the last *verse*.

gloss: A short pattern of notes repeated through a rock or jazz song.
examples: That guitar *riff* is instantly recognizable.
He built the whole song around one *riff*.
The band jammed on a couple of *riffs* for ten minutes.

gloss: A musician or singer who performs alone in front of a group.
examples: The *soloist* got a standing ovation.
She was the *soloist* in the second piece.
Both *soloists* were students at the conservatory.

gloss: A piece of music for two performers.
examples: They sang a *duet* at the end of the show.
The *duet* is written for flute and piano.
We practiced our *duet* all week.

gloss: A group of four musicians, or a piece written for four of them.
examples: A string *quartet* played during dinner.
The *quartet* has been together for twenty years.
Two *quartets* are on the program tonight.

gloss: A small group of musicians who perform together.
examples: She plays in a small jazz *ensemble*.
The *ensemble* rehearses on Thursday nights.
The school has three student *ensembles*.
contrast: From French: ahn-SAHM-buhl, with the final e silent.

gloss: The person who stands in front of an orchestra and directs the players.
examples: The *conductor* stopped the orchestra and started over.
She's the youngest *conductor* they have ever hired.
Both *conductors* studied in Vienna.

gloss: Someone who writes music.
examples: The *composer* died before the opera was finished.
She's a *composer* of film music.
Living *composers* rarely get played at these concerts.

gloss: The written music for all the parts of a piece, or music written for a film.
examples: The pianist turned the pages of the *score*.
He wrote the *score* for three films last year.
The *scores* are kept in the library downstairs.

gloss: Printed pages of music that a performer reads from.
examples: She keeps her *sheet music* in a black folder.
You can buy the *sheet music* online for a few dollars.
He plays by ear and never uses *sheet music*.
contrast: Uncountable: *some sheet music* or *a piece of sheet music* — never *a sheet music*.

gloss: The words of a song.
examples: The *lyrics* are printed inside the album cover.
He writes the *lyrics* and she writes the music.
Nobody can understand the *lyrics* on that track.
contrast: Used in the plural — *the lyrics are* — almost never *a lyric*.

gloss: A short piece of music with words that are sung.
examples: That *song* was on the radio all summer.
She wrote the *song* in an afternoon.
They played all their old *songs* at the end.

gloss: Someone who writes the words and music of songs.
examples: He's a better *songwriter* than a singer.
The *songwriters* got most of the money.
She's a working *songwriter* in Nashville.

gloss: Someone who sings, plays, or acts in front of an audience.
examples: The *performer* came back out for one more number.
Street *performers* fill the square all summer.
She's a natural *performer*.

gloss: A public performance of music.
examples: We're going to a *concert* on Friday.
The *concert* starts at eight sharp.
They played sixty *concerts* last year.
contrast: *Concert* (KAHN-surt) is an event; a *concerto* (kuhn-CHER-toh) is a piece of music.

gloss: A small concert given by one performer or by students.
examples: Her piano *recital* is on Sunday afternoon.
Every student plays one piece at the *recital*.
The *recitals* are held in the school gym.

gloss: A single paid performance by a musician or band.
examples: The band has a *gig* at a bar downtown.
He plays about forty *gigs* a year.
The *gig* paid two hundred dollars and a free meal.

gloss: The building or place where a concert or event is held.
examples: The *venue* holds about a thousand people.
They moved the show to a bigger *venue*.
Small *venues* are closing all over the city.

gloss: The raised floor where musicians or actors perform.
examples: The band walked out on *stage* at nine.
She was nervous the first time she stood on a *stage*.
The festival has four *stages* running at once.

gloss: The sound of an audience clapping to show they liked something.
examples: The *applause* went on for five minutes.
There was polite *applause* and then silence.
She waited for the *applause* to die down.
contrast: Uncountable in English even though Russian аплодисменты is plural: *the applause was* deafening.

gloss: An extra piece performed at the end of a show because the audience asks for it.
examples: The band came back out for one *encore*.
The crowd shouted until they played an *encore*.
She did two *encores* and still nobody left.
contrast: From French: AHN-kor, with the first syllable nasal-sounding and stressed.

gloss: A practice session before a performance.
examples: *Rehearsal* is at six on Tuesday.
We had exactly one *rehearsal* before the show.
The *rehearsals* ran long all week.

gloss: A short performance given to see whether someone is good enough for a part.
examples: She has an *audition* for the orchestra next week.
The *audition* lasted about four minutes.
Hundreds of people showed up for the *auditions*.

gloss: All the pieces a performer or group knows and can play.
examples: The band's *repertoire* is mostly old soul.
She added two new pieces to her *repertoire*.
Their *repertoires* barely overlap.
contrast: French spelling, said REP-ur-twar — the -toire is not read as English.

gloss: A long piece of music in several parts, written for a full orchestra.
examples: The *symphony* has four movements.
He wrote nine *symphonies* in thirty years.
We heard his fifth *symphony* live last month.

gloss: A piece of classical music for one or two instruments, usually in three parts.
examples: She's learning a Beethoven *sonata*.
The *sonata* is written for violin and piano.
He recorded all thirty-two piano *sonatas*.

gloss: The orchestral piece played at the beginning of an opera or a show.
examples: The *overture* is the best-known part of the opera.
The orchestra opened with a short *overture*.
Both *overtures* were written after the operas were finished.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A play in which the words are sung, or this art form in general.
examples: We saw an *opera* in Italian with subtitles.
She has loved *opera* since she was a kid.
The company puts on three *operas* a season.

gloss: A song for one voice in an opera.
examples: The soprano's *aria* stopped the show.
That *aria* is on every audition list.
He knows the *arias* by heart.

gloss: A slow song, or an old song that tells a story.
examples: The album ends with a slow *ballad*.
The old *ballad* tells the story of a shipwreck.
They play *ballads* at the end of the night.

gloss: A song that stands for a country or a group, sung on important occasions.
examples: The crowd stood for the national *anthem*.
That song became an *anthem* for a whole generation.
Both *anthems* were played before the game.

gloss: A religious song sung by a congregation in church.
examples: The congregation sang an old *hymn*.
She played *hymns* on the organ every Sunday.
The *hymn* numbers are posted on the board.
contrast: The n is silent: HIM, exactly like *him*.

gloss: A Christmas song.
examples: The kids sang *carols* outside the church.
My favorite Christmas *carol* is that quiet one.
They go door to door singing *carols* every December.

gloss: A quiet song sung to help a baby fall asleep.
examples: She sang the baby a *lullaby*.
He knows two *lullabies* in Russian.
The whole song is really just a *lullaby*.

gloss: A piece of music in three beats to a measure, written for dancing.
examples: They danced a slow *waltz*.
The band played a *waltz* to close the night.
He wrote dozens of *waltzes*.

gloss: A piece of music with a strong steady beat, written for marching.
examples: The band played a *march* down Main Street.
That *march* gets played at every graduation.
Sousa wrote over a hundred *marches*.

gloss: A style of American music built on improvising over a rhythm section.
examples: He listens to *jazz* while he works.
The club has live *jazz* on weekends.
*Jazz* came out of New Orleans.

gloss: A slow, sad style of American music that grew out of the rural South.
examples: He plays *blues* on a beat-up guitar.
The *blues* came up the river from the Delta.
That song is straight *blues*.
contrast: Looks plural but takes a singular verb: *the blues is* an American form.

gloss: A flat black disc that music is played from, or an album of recorded music.
examples: He still buys *records* instead of streaming.
The *record* skipped on the second track.
She has a whole wall of *records*.
contrast: The noun is REK-urd; the verb *to record* is rih-KORD.

gloss: Music or sound that has been captured so it can be played back.
examples: The *recording* was made in an old church.
There are three *recordings* of that symphony.
This *recording* has by far the best sound.

gloss: The music that goes with a film or a game.
examples: The *soundtrack* is better than the movie.
He composed the *soundtrack* in two weeks.
She owns the *soundtracks* to all of them.

gloss: A list of songs put in order to be played one after another.
examples: I made a *playlist* for the drive.
Her *playlist* is all nineties hip-hop.
The bar has a great *playlist*.

gloss: A style of music built on rapped words over a strong beat.
examples: He grew up on *hip-hop*.
The station plays *hip-hop* all afternoon.
*Hip-hop* started in the Bronx in the seventies.

gloss: A musician who plays the drums.
examples: The *drummer* counted them in.
They're looking for a new *drummer*.
Both *drummers* played at once on that track.

gloss: A musician who plays the guitar.
examples: The *guitarist* broke a string in the middle of the song.
She's the best *guitarist* in town.
Two *guitarists* traded solos for ten minutes.

gloss: A musician who plays the piano.
examples: The *pianist* played the whole set without sheet music.
She's a concert *pianist*.
The two *pianists* took turns at the same piano.
contrast: Most Americans say pee-AN-ist, with the stress on the second syllable.

gloss: A musician who plays the violin.
examples: The *violinist* tuned up before everyone else.
He's a *violinist* with the city orchestra.
Four *violinists* auditioned for one seat.

gloss: A gradual rise in loudness in a piece of music.
examples: The music builds to a huge *crescendo*.
The *crescendo* at the end shakes the whole room.
There are two *crescendos* on the final page.
contrast: The sc is pronounced sh, from Italian: kruh-SHEN-doh.

gloss: The highest singing voice, or a singer with that voice.
examples: The *soprano* hit the high note easily.
She sings *soprano* in the church choir.
The *sopranos* stand on the left.

gloss: The lower female singing voice, or a singer with that voice.
examples: She sings *alto* in the choir.
The *altos* come in on the second line.
He wrote the part for *alto* and piano.

gloss: The higher male singing voice, or a singer with that voice.
examples: The *tenor* got the loudest applause of the night.
He sings *tenor* in a barbershop group.
Three *tenors* shared the role that season.
